notes.h: The individual and group dance requirement
notes.b: Dance is an aesthetic activity, one where the movement is judged for how it looks and what it expresses. Learners perform it twice, once alone and once in a group, and the same areas are considered in both.
points: Learners perform an individual dance and a group dance, so they must be able to perform on their own and to dance with others.
Both dances show consideration of technical ability, choreographic design (how the dance is planned and put together), dance style, props and music, and overall sense of performance.

Choreographic design includes choreographic content (what movements and space the dance uses), choreographic construction (how a motif is built up and varied) and choreographic form (the overall structure of the dance).
notes.tip: Dance is a common aesthetic activity in written answers, so be ready to apply compositional elements and aesthetic and artistic criteria to it. Those criteria are taught elsewhere; here you apply them to dance.

notes.b: Technical ability is how well the body is used to perform the movements. It is made up of eight skills, and each one has a clear meaning you can describe in an answer.
points: Posture: an upright, lifted carriage of the body, which gives a clean line for every movement.
Alignment: body parts held in a correct line, for example knees over toes.
Co-ordination: movements of different body parts combined in time, so that arms, legs and trunk work together.
Balance: holding the body steady over its base (the part of the body in contact with the floor).
Strength: the muscular power to lift, hold and control the body.
Flexibility: the ability of muscles and joints to move through a large range.
Mobility: the range of movement available at each joint (a joint is where two bones meet).
Control: stopping, holding and moving precisely, rather than letting momentum carry the body.

notes.b: Choreography is the planning and arranging of dance movement. Its content is the raw material the choreographer works with: space, time and the other dancers.
points: Levels: high, medium and low positions, which add variety by moving the dancer up and down in space.
Pathways: straight, curved and zigzag routes across the floor.
Directions and formations: the way dancers face and how they are arranged, such as in lines or circles.
Timing: the speed, rhythm and stillness of movement, so a pause is part of the timing as well as movement.
Relationships to other dancers: mirroring (copying a partner as in a mirror), contrast, leading and following, and contact.
notes.tip: Levels, pathways and timing count as compositional elements, so use them when an answer asks you to analyse choreography.

notes.b: Once the content is chosen, a choreographer builds the dance from a small idea that is then developed. That idea is the motif.
points: A motif is a short movement phrase (a short sequence of linked movements) that expresses the theme, so it carries the idea of the dance.
Variation changes the motif so it does not simply repeat unchanged, for example by altering its size, speed, level, direction or body part.
Adding repetition is also a way of varying a motif, because repeating it in a new place or with a new emphasis changes how it is seen.

notes.b: Form is the overall structure of a dance, in the way a song has verses and a chorus. It describes whether dancers move together or in turn, and how sections are ordered. A letter stands for each section, so AB means two different sections.
points: Unison: all dancers perform the same movement at the same time, for example a group arm sweep done together on one beat.
Canon: dancers perform the same movement one after another, as in a round, for example each dancer starting the same sequence a few counts after the one before.
Binary (AB): two contrasting sections, for example a slow, smooth section followed by a fast, sharp one.
Ternary (ABA): three sections in which the first returns after a contrasting middle, for example a slow opening, a fast middle and the opening returning.
Rondo (ABACA): a main section A returns between contrasting sections B and C, for example a main group phrase returning between a duet and a solo.
notes.tip: Canon is sequential and unison is simultaneous, so do not swap them. Unison, canon, binary, ternary and rondo are the standard forms.

notes.b: A dance style is a recognised type of dance with its own movement, music and history. Each of the eight styles on the syllabus can be identified by one defining feature.
points: Contemporary: draws on ballet and modern techniques and uses fluid, expressive movement and floor work (movement performed on or close to the floor).
Folk: social dance of ordinary people, usually performed in groups and passed on informally.
Modern: a style that broke away from classical ballet conventions, using contraction (a tightening of the body), release and floor work.
Ballet: a classical style with turnout (legs rotated outward from the hips), pointed feet, set positions and a codified vocabulary of steps (a fixed, named set of steps).
Jazz: an energetic style with sharp, rhythmic movements and isolations of body parts (moving one part while the rest stays still), often danced to jazz music.
Tap: a style in which metal plates on the shoes make percussive sounds as the dancer steps and taps.
Ethnic: a style rooted in the dance of a particular cultural group, performed with that group's music and costume.
Traditional: a style passed down through generations within a community, such as Irish traditional dance.

notes.b: Props and music support the movement and help the dance communicate its theme. The dancer must use both deliberately, and not let them distract from the dancing.
points: Props extend the movement or tell part of the story, for example a chair, a scarf or a ribbon.
Music sets the mood, tempo (speed) and structure of the dance, so it shapes how the audience feels and where sections begin and end.
Movement is matched to the phrasing (the musical sentences) and accents (the stressed beats) of the music.
Silence can be used for effect, because the absence of music draws attention to the movement.

notes.b: A dance is for an audience, so the overall sense of performance matters as well as the steps. Performers must communicate the theme artistically and aesthetically, meaning in a way that is expressive and pleasing to watch.
points: Projection: energy and expression sent out to the audience, so that even those at the back can see and feel the dance.
Focus: where the eyes look, which directs the audience's attention.
Facial expression matches the theme, so the face supports the story of the dance.
Energy and commitment are shown in every movement, not only in the big moments.
Confidence is shown in the performance, and the theme is communicated to the audience artistically and aesthetically.
notes.tip: Aesthetic and artistic criteria are taught elsewhere. When asked about dance, apply them by naming specific features such as projection, focus and facial expression.

notes.b: A choreographer does not create a finished dance in one go. The work follows a sequence of stages from first idea to polished performance.
points: 1. Choose a stimulus (the starting idea, such as a picture or a piece of music) or theme.
2. Improvise (try out movement freely without planning) and select the movement that works best.
3. Create motifs from the selected movement.
4. Develop and structure the motifs into a chosen form, such as binary or rondo.
5. Rehearse, then refine using feedback and video, because watching a recording shows what the dancer cannot see while performing.

notes.b: Dance puts demands on the joints and muscles, and dancers move close together, so injury is a risk. These five habits keep dancers safe.
points: Warm-up and cool-down are both part of safe practice, one before and one after the dance.
The floor surface and footwear must be suitable, so that dancers do not slip or strain their joints.
Dancers keep enough space between them, so they do not collide.
Lifts and landings use correct technique, because poor technique in these moments risks injury.
Hydration is maintained, meaning dancers drink enough water.

notes.b: Dance asks for a mix of physical, skill-related and personal qualities. The group dance adds one more, working with others.
points: Flexibility, balance and strength are needed to perform the movements.
Muscular endurance (the ability of muscles to keep working without tiring) is needed to sustain a dance.
Co-ordination, rhythm and spatial awareness (knowing where you and others are in the space) are needed.
Confidence and expression are required to perform in front of an audience.
Teamwork is needed in the group dance, so that dancers move together.
notes.tip: When comparing dance with another activity, link each demand to the part of the dance that calls for it.

keyTerms.definition: A short movement phrase that expresses the theme of a dance and is developed by the choreographer.
A change made to a motif, such as its size, speed, level, direction or body part, or the addition of repetition.
A choreographic form in which all dancers perform the same movement at the same time.
A choreographic form in which dancers perform the same movement one after another, as in a round.
A choreographic form with two contrasting sections, A then B.
A choreographic form with three sections in the pattern A B A.
A choreographic form in which a main section A returns between contrasting sections, as in A B A C A.
The height of a movement: high, medium or low.
The route a dancer takes across the floor, such as straight, curved or zigzag.
The correct line of the body parts, such as knees over toes.
The range of movement available at each joint.
An idea or starting point, such as a theme, from which movement is created.
The use of space, timing and relationships to other dancers within a dance.

factCards.definition: Unison is simultaneous, with all dancers moving at the same time; canon is sequential, with each dancer starting after the one before.

factCards.term: Five choreographic forms named in the specification
factCards.definition: Unison, canon, binary (AB), ternary (ABA) and rondo (ABACA).
Posture, alignment, co-ordination, balance, strength, flexibility, mobility and control.
Levels: high, medium and low. Pathways: straight, curved and zigzag.

factCards.term: Six stages of the choreographic process
factCards.definition: Choose a stimulus, improvise and select movement, create motifs, develop and structure them into a form, rehearse, then refine with feedback and video.

factCards.term: Eight dance styles in the specification
factCards.definition: Contemporary, folk, modern, ballet, jazz, tap, ethnic and traditional.

questions.prompt: Explain three choreographic devices or forms a choreographer could use in a group dance, with an example of each.
questions.model: Unison: all dancers perform the same movement at the same time, for example a sequence of arm sweeps performed together on the same beat. This gives the group a strong sense of unity. Canon: each dancer performs the same movement one after another, as in a round, for example a step and arm wave passed from dancer to dancer, each starting a few counts after the last. This spreads one idea across the whole group over time. Rondo (ABACA): a main section A returns between contrasting sections B and C, for example a main group phrase returning between a duet and a solo section. This gives the dance a clear structure and keeps the main theme recognisable throughout.

questions.prompt: Explain motif and variation in dance.
questions.model: A motif is a short movement phrase that expresses the theme of the dance, and it is the basic building block that the choreographer develops. Variation is the change made to a motif to develop it, such as altering its size, speed, level or direction, changing the body part used, or adding repetition. For example, a motif of a step, an arm sweep and a turn can be varied by performing it at a low level, performing it faster, or using the legs instead of the arms. The same idea returns in changed form, so the dance has both unity and development.
